extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, parties and experts in IPRs (PTAB), patent litigators and in-house counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evaluative criteria used by the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB) to determine anticipation, enablement, and obviousness (including objective indicia) of patent claims in an inter partes review. Covers how prior-art disclosures, expert testimony, inherency, nexus, coextensiveness, motivation to combine, and reasonable expectation of success are weighed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation — disclosure of every claim limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: In an anticipation analysis, the dispositive question is whether a skilled artisan would 'reasonably understand or infer' from a prior art reference that every claim limitation is disclosed in that single reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expert testimony may shed light on what a skilled artisan would reasonably understand or infer from a prior art reference (Acoustic Tech., Inc. v. Itron Networked Sols., Inc.). Anticipation requires that every limitation is disclosed 'arranged as in the claim' (Net MoneyIN, Inc. v. VeriSign, Inc.). Inherency can establish anticipation when the missing limitation is necessarily present or would be recognized by the POSA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement of prior art disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior-art reference need not have actually made or tested a nucleotide sequence (or other embodiment) if the reference discloses it and making it would have been well within the skill of one of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enablement is satisfied if the disclosure allows a POSA to make the claimed subject matter without undue experimentation. Routine matters (e.g., converting protein sequence to nucleotide sequence) support enablement (In re Wallach; Bristol-Myers Squibb v. Ben Venue Labs.). Citations and statements in the prior art that established 'well known genetic engineering techniques' can show enablement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness — Graham framework and consideration of entire record
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentability (obviousness) is determined based on the entirety of the evidence before the factfinder, both for and against obviousness, using the Graham factors (including scope/contents of prior art, differences, level of ordinary skill, and objective indicia).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objective evidence of non-obviousness (secondary considerations) may often be highly probative but does not necessarily control the outcome. The Board weighs all evidence (e.g., Transocean, Pfizer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective indicia of nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognized categories include long-felt need and failure of others, praise and copying by others, and unexpected results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such evidence may be the most probative but requires a nexus to the claimed invention; it must be reasonably commensurate with the scope of the claims (ClassCo v. Apple; Rambus). Examples: evidence of industry adoption, clinical success, or unexpected superior efficacy can be offered under these categories but must be tied to the claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nexus requirement between objective evidence and claimed invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee must establish a legally and factually sufficient connection (nexus) between the objective evidence and the merits of the claimed invention for the objective indicia to be given weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A presumption of nexus arises when the patentee shows the asserted objective evidence is tied to a specific product that 'embodies the claimed features, and is coextensive with them' (Fox Factory; Polaris). If nexus is not presumed, the patentee may still prove nexus by showing the evidence is the direct result of the unique characteristics of the claimed invention (In re Huang). Evidence directed to a feature already in the prior art (not novel in the claim) lacks nexus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coextensiveness/commensurate-in-scope standard for presumption of nexus
rubrics_metrics.description: A presumption of nexus is appropriate only when the marketed product embodies the claimed features and is coextensive (i.e., the product is essentially the claimed invention; unclaimed features are insignificant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coextensive means the product is the invention disclosed and claimed; unclaimed features must amount to nothing more than insignificant additions (Campbell Soup; Fox Factory; Zaxcom discussion). If a product includes significant differences (e.g., specific capsid, promoter), presumption may not apply and nexus may be weak or absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherency in anticipation and obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: A limitation may be inherently disclosed by a reference when a skilled artisan would necessarily recognize that limitation from the disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example from record: because Stafford discloses administering an AAV vector to patients, a POSA would recognize the vector would necessarily be administered in a pharmaceutical composition, so claim reciting 'pharmaceutical composition comprising the vector' can be inherently disclosed. Expert testimony can support inherency findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not import intended-use or functional limitations into product claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Product claims should not be limited by asserted intended uses or by reading functional limitations into the claim when those limitations are not recited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent Owner's attempt to import functional limitations (e.g., 'vector is used to introduce a nucleic acid into a cell for expression') into a product claim was rejected. For product claims lacking functional language, the evaluation focuses on structural limitations disclosed in the prior art, not on the patentee's asserted purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation to combine prior art references
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish obviousness over multiple references, a party must show that a POSA would have been motivated to combine the references to arrive at the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motivation may be supported by express teachings, industry context (e.g., use of AAV vectors in hemophilia gene therapy), or known advantages (e.g., improved activity of a variant). The Board examines whether prior art and contemporaneous knowledge would have provided the rationale to modify or combine teachings with a reasonable expectation of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable expectation of success
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if motivated to combine references, obviousness requires that a POSA would have had a reasonable expectation that the combination would work for its intended purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence that modifications were routine and within ordinary skill supports reasonable expectation (e.g., routine conversion of sequences, standard vector construction). Conversely, unpredictability of expression/activity or lack of data may undermine an expectation of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof allocation in IPR objective indicia
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee bears the burden to establish nexus for objective indicia; if a presumption of nexus is shown, the burden shifts to the challenger to rebut it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the patentee cannot establish nexus or coextensiveness, objective indicia carry less weight. Case citations: ClassCo, Fox Factory, Brown & Williamson, Merck (on limits of weak nexus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art is read 'for all that it teaches'
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior-art reference is relevant not only for its principal focus but for all teachings it provides that a POSA would understand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re Mouttet: a reference's larger focus (e.g., protein replacement therapy) does not negate its teaching of other relevant aspects (e.g., gene therapy and AAV vectors) if those teachings are present in the disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective indicia insufficient if directed to features already in the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective evidence (praise, copying, unexpected results) directed to a feature that was already known in the prior art does not establish nonobviousness of the claimed invention as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: praise directed to FIX-R338L itself (which Stafford disclosed) cannot establish nexus for claims covering AAV-FIX-R338L combinations. The Board will discount objective indicia that are attributable to previously known elements.
